thread.title: Apple: Everyone Wants To Be A Value Investor, Until Crunch Time - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Michael Wiggins De Oliveira
title: Apple: Everyone Wants To Be A Value Investor, Until Crunch Time - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Investment Thesis Apple ( AAPL ) has terrific free cash flow, yet an abundance of data from different news outlets is causing investors to act with irrational fear. I urge readers to remember that when they buy Apple's stock, they are not buying pieces of paper, but that they are instead buying a portion of Apple's future profitability.
Apple is undervalued any way a rational and objective investor appraises this investment.
What Is Buffett Doing?
It's not supposed to be easy. Anyone who finds it easy is stupid.
- Charlie Munger; Vice Chairman of Berkshire Hathaway
In the past three months, we have seen Apple lose a third of market cap value. Do you honestly think that Warren Buffett is worried about his investment? Do think that he has lost any sleep over this fact? I trust that you will find the answer is no. And the reason being that Buffett has taught us time and time again, that the market is there to serves us, and not the other way round. Buffett has taught us endless parables over the years about Mr. Market's antics .
Mr. Market has another endearing characteristic: He doesn’t mind being ignored. If his quotation is uninteresting to you today, he will be back with a new one tomorrow. Transactions are strictly at your option . Under these conditions, the more manic-depressive his behavior, the better for you.
Further, Buffett has laid out the path towards strong market returns. That the best way to achieve market-beating results is through patience. Through doing nothing. But giving business time to deliver strong profitable earnings to its owners.
Slow Diversification, Yet Meaningful iPhones are obviously vital to Apple's consolidated revenue growth. The product is fantastic; this is undeniable. However, common sense dictates that while iPhones are crucial, they are not the full story.
CEO Tim Cook's letter highlights that this quarter's performance was not going to be as strong as many had hoped for. But investors should not overly focus on quarter-to-quarter comparisons.
Cook specifically highlights that Apple will be shifting its energy towards its loyal installed base, that Apple's Services segment continues to deliver growth to Apple and is expected to continue to do so for the foreseeable future.
No rational investor should downplay the importance of iPhone sales which accounts for approximately 63% of Apple's total revenue. However, my point is that investors had already somewhat expected that the law of large numbers to start to become an insurmountable hurdle for Apple. Let's look at this from aside - investors have not been paying a premium for Apple for a significant amount of time, right?
Investors were already largely bracing themselves that it would be a challenge to keep pushing iPhone revenue higher. Now, on the plus side, the margins from Services will be materially improved, when compared with the sale of hardware. Plus, at the end of the day, no matter how efficient Apple is with its manufacturing and distribution of its hardware, this can't compare with sending a software around the globe - it is simply not in the same ballpark.
Said another way, in spite of having to deal with less revenue than expected in Q1 2019, Cook's letter states that Apple's gross margin is still expected to reach approximately 38%, compared with the original 38% and 38.5% given during the earnings call at the end of Q4 2018.
In more detail, Cook's letter highlights that Services revenue is likely to be up roughly 27.5% in Q1 2019 compared with the same period a year ago. In other words, this is vindication that not only is Apple truly diversifying away from its dependency on iPhone sales for future revenue growth. But that Apple's management team continues to be top-class, and finding opportunities for growth in a maturing smartphone environment.
Valuation In a final attempt to drive home my point that Apple is undervalued, allow me to once again put a spotlight on Apple's management team. Rather than being caught flat-footed, when their flagship product inevitably slowed down, management had the foresight years ago to leverage its ecosystem to be a value-added service-oriented product.
For this moment, right now, Apple has been preparing for more than 5 years in the background. Apple, unlike many other tech companies, is notoriously tight-lipped about their ongoing projects until the time is right to ramp up and execute.
Moreover, going back to Q1 2017 , Apple then, at that point, was already aggressively strategizing how its Services segment should double in size by FY 2020. In fact, already now, to put Apple's Q1 2019 service revenue in perspective, Apple has forecast the quarter to generate $10.8 billion from its Services. This is roughly two and a half times more revenue than Netflix ( NFLX ) is expected to have generated over the past quarter. Furthermore, Netflix's long-term outlook expects Netflix's operating margin to reach 13%, which is paltry in comparison with Apple's mid-20% being generated right now.
In other words, right now, Apple shareholders are essentially getting twice the revenue from Netflix, at twice the profitability, bundled in with Apple's portfolio of business, essentially for free when they buy Apple right now.
Source: Author's calculations, morningstar.com
Once again, the table highlights just how undervalued Apple is. Not only is Apple undervalued relative to its peers, but it's also clearly undervalued relative to itself.
Takeaway Investors have become disenchanted with Apple's lack of growth. However, the fact of the matter is that presently, Apple shareholders are not being asked to pay for any growth.
Over time, businesses go through their own vicissitudes, and the best time to buy them is when others won't. Apple's cash flows currently trade at single digits. Furthermore, I believe that over the next 2 years, Apple's dependency over its iPhone will continue to dwindle. And at that time, once again, Mr. Market will return, fully spirited and passionate for Apple, causing Apple's shares to reprice higher.
